cards.title: Untenable stalemate
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This is a critical study of regional geopolitics and the limitations of diplomacy in the face of shifting US foreign policy.
cards.summary: The ongoing US-Iran conflict remains a dangerous stalemate that threatens regional stability. While Pakistan continues to push for a diplomatic settlement, inconsistent messaging from the White House hampers these efforts. Recent military exchanges demonstrate the risk of an accidental escalation into a broader confrontation.
key_facts: Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar confirmed Pakistan's continued pursuit of a negotiated peace.
The Iranian foreign minister visited Islamabad for the Economic Cooperation Organization meeting.
Recent military engagements included US strikes on Iranian coastal facilities and Iranian strikes on US sites in Bahrain.
The editorial identifies US policy as suffering from cognitive dissonance regarding the status of the war.

vocab.meaning: A situation where neither side in a conflict can make progress.
Mental conflict caused by holding contradictory beliefs or values.
To move or swing between two points or opinions.

text: NEARLY nine months into a conflict of choice that has rattled economies from Europe to Asia, there seem to be few agreeable options for the US where ending the Iran war is concerned.

No one — perhaps apart from Israel and some hawks in Washington — wants an escalation, while coming to an agreement on Iran’s terms would result in considerable embarrassment for Donald Trump. However, Pakistan, which has played a crucial mediatory role in the conflict, and other regional states still have expectations that a negotiated settlement can be reached. As Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar told the ECO meeting on Monday, “we have not given up hope” for peace. The Iranian foreign minister was also in Islamabad for the event, and praised Pakistan’s efforts to broker peace.

But the most sincere efforts by Pakistan or any other mediator will not bear fruit unless there is clarity in Washington. President Trump, as has been his practice, has oscillated between saying the war is “effectively over”, and threatening fresh strikes if talks fall through. This cognitive dissonance must end.

Over the past few days, there have been some low-key military engagements between the US and Iran. The US had reportedly attacked facilities on the Iranian coast, while Tehran hit back by targeting American sites in Bahrain. These exchanges have the potential to get out of hand and spark a bigger confrontation. Which is why the quicker the matter is resolved, the better.

The collective voice from the states of this region is clearly against war, while the majority of the American people also appear uninterested in fresh clashes with Iran. Therefore, it is time the White House faced the bitter reality that its ill-conceived Iran campaign — fuelled by bad Israeli advice — has failed, and committed to resolving the imbroglio peacefully.

The option of attacking Iran again must be taken off the table by the US. In fact, there should be a positive response to the Iranian proposal currently on the table, specifically where lifting the blockade, ending sanctions, and allowing access to Tehran’s funds goes. This may seem like ‘capitulation’ to Mr Trump, but these matters should have been thought through before launching this disastrous war.

Tehran should also show flexibility, particularly where free and unhindered access through the Strait of Hormuz is concerned. Should Washington opt for the diplomatic off-ramp, it will find that regional states, particularly Pakistan, Qatar and others, will be happy to facilitate dialogue. However, indecision and a damaging status quo that is affecting regional peace and the global economy cannot be allowed to continue. It is time the Trump administration did the right thing.
Published in Dawn, November 18th, 2026

cards.title: Cricket hegemony
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This illustrates the intersection of geopolitics and international sports governance, a common theme in Current Affairs.
cards.summary: India's dominance in international cricket governance has led to Pakistan being excluded from hosting major events until 2031. The International Cricket Council, now led by Indian officials, has awarded all major tournament rights to India and other partner nations. This reflects a broader trend of political tension overriding sports diplomacy between the two countries.
key_facts: The ICC announced its activity program for the 2028-2035 cycle.
Jay Shah serves as the chairman of the ICC.
Sanoj Gupta serves as the CEO of the ICC.
India will co-host the 2031 ODI World Cup with Bangladesh.
The 2028 T20 World Cup will be hosted by Australia and New Zealand.

vocab.meaning: Dominance of one group or country over others.
Given or done in return for something else.
Engaging in political activity or maneuvering.

text: ANY doubts over India’s total hegemony over world cricket have now been removed. Its tactic of sidelining Pakistan is more blatant than ever.
The India-led International Cricket Council on Sunday announced its activity programme for the 2028-2035 cycle and conveniently left Pakistan without hosting rights for any event until 2031.

The ICC, chaired by former Board of Control for Cricket in India secretary Jay Shah — who was re-elected unopposed for another term on Monday — and run by his fellow countryman Sanoj Gupta as the chief executive officer, unveiled venues for major world tournaments over the next five years and split them between India, England, Australia and New Zealand.

Australia and New Zealand were confirmed as hosts of the next T20 World Cup in 2028. The 2030 T20 showpiece will be hosted by England, Ireland and Scotland. England will also host the World Test Championship finals in 2029 and 2031. India, meanwhile, have been awarded hosting rights for the 2029 Champions Trophy while they will co-host the 2031 ODI World Cup with Bangladesh.

These decisions come despite Pakistan successfully hosting the Champions Trophy last year, where India’s politicking saw matches of its team shifted to Dubai and the final also being hosted there. That move saw the Pakistan Cricket Board agree to a reciprocal deal with the BCCI where Pakistan’s matches in ICC events hosted by India for the next five years would also be played at neutral venues, and it is also probably the rationale behind making Bangladesh co-hosts for the 2031 ODI World Cup.

Political ties between India and Pakistan remain strained and the former has not shied away from bringing the heat onto the pitch on several occasions. Politics will likely spill over once again if Pakistan qualify for the 2029 Champions Trophy in India.
India has pulled out all the stops in its blatant sidelining of Pakistan and the burning question remains whether cricket will be able to rise from all of this.
Published in Dawn, November 18th, 2026

cards.title: Poor treatment
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This touches on the rule of law, the role of the judiciary, and human rights standards in Pakistan's governance.
cards.summary: A former prime minister has petitioned the judiciary for urgent medical attention for himself and his wife. While the government claims the prisoners are receiving adequate care, the editorial argues for transparency and adherence to court-mandated medical access. It emphasizes the need for the state to uphold basic human rights regardless of political disputes.
key_facts: Imran Khan submitted a letter to the Federal Constitutional Court, Supreme Court, and Islamabad High Court.
The letter requested medical care due to risks of brain haemorrhage and potential loss of eyesight for his spouse.
Lawyer Salman Safdar drafted the letter on behalf of the former prime minister.
The Supreme Court issued a directive in August regarding medical examination for the prisoners.

vocab.meaning: To ask someone urgently and fervently to do something.
A political system or authority in power.
Making a statement more interesting or dramatic by adding extra details.

text: IT is unseemly that a jailed political leader is forced to beseech the chief justices of the Federal Constitutional Court, the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court for medical attention.

In an open letter issued Monday, former prime minister Imran Khan detailed his and his wife’s medical condition, claiming he faces heightened risk of brain haemorrhage while his spouse could lose her eyesight.

“I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive. I appeal to your Lordships, on the most basic grounds of human compassion: give me justice before it is too late,” reads his letter, penned on his behalf by his lawyer, Salman Safdar.

The government still disputes this, and insists that the two continue to receive adequate medical attention. In fact, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, responding to the letter, said Mr Khan is “[…] among the most privileged prisoners in Pakistan,” while telling the PTI to stop “politicising his health”.

But even if government ministers believe the former PM is embellishing the facts, what is the harm in allowing him a medical examination under the supervision of his physicians, as the SC directed in August ?

Some may argue that the many difficulties Mr Khan finds himself in are self-created. There are many in the ruling dispensation who believe that what is being done to him is ‘justice’, considering that he, too, had victimised his opponents during his time in power. Mr Khan’s speeches about depriving his jailed political opponents of various facilities and amenities granted to them have not been forgotten in those circles.
Still, as far as Mr Khan and his wife’s health is concerned, the government must show compassion, if not respect for their rights.

The courts have given the state grounds to deprive Mr Khan and his spouse of their liberty, not their health. If the two prisoners are complaining that their treatment has not been adequate, the government can allow those needs to be met to their satisfaction without making any change to their status as prisoners. There is no conceivable harm in making such an allowance.
Those in power today should also think about the precedent they are setting. Do they want to be treated similarly in the future? The cycle of revenge needs to stop, and compassion alone can break it.
Published in Dawn, November 18th, 2026
